name: Mexican or Mexican-American
blurb: Family, faith and music. Many couples include padrinos (sponsors), the lazo and the arras. Every family does it a little differently, so keep what fits yours.

lines.note: A cord of flowers or a large rosary placed around the couple after the vows. Padrinos often give it as a gift, so ask before you buy one.

lines.item: Arras (13 coins) and the box or tray
lines.note: 13 gold coins the groom gives the bride. For Catholic couples they sit in a decorated box or tray the priest blesses. The box is usually a padrino gift. Ask your padrinos first.
White pillows decorated with lace, for kneeling during Mass. Padrinos usually give them, and the couple keeps them. Ask before you buy.
Padrinos may pay for a Bible, along with the lazo and kneeling pillows. Ask which gifts each one is giving so nothing is bought twice.
A traditional cake can be served with other sweets such as flan, tres leches cake and churros. Skip this line if your cake is enough.
A smaller gathering of close family and friends after the main reception. Decide who is invited and who pays.

milestones.title: Choose your padrinos and what each one covers
milestones.short: Padrinos help with the ceremony and may pay for parts of it.

steps.title: Pick people you trust
steps.body: Padrinos and madrinas are chosen for their bond with you. One guide says there are no fixed roles and you can choose as many as you like.

steps.title: Ask what each would like to give
steps.body: Padrinos may cover the lazo, arras, kneeling pillows or a Bible. Some couples also name padrinos for flowers, cake, rings, music, photos or the dress. Ask before you buy any of these yourself.

steps.title: Write down who covers what
steps.body: Add each promise to Who is helping in Padrino. That way nothing gets bought twice and nobody is left guessing.

milestones.title: Plan the lazo, arras and other ceremony items
milestones.short: Know who is bringing what before the rehearsal.

steps.title: Lazo
steps.body: Ask if your padrinos are giving it. If not, get one made of flowers or a rosary. It goes around your shoulders after the vows.

steps.title: Arras
steps.body: Decide who is buying the 13 coins and the box or tray. For a Catholic wedding the priest blesses them.

steps.title: Ask your priest how it works
steps.body: If you marry in a church, ask how the lazo, the arras and the Mass fit together. The priest removes the lazo at the end.

milestones.title: Plan the mariachi and the tornaboda
milestones.short: Music at the ceremony, the reception and after.

steps.title: Mariachi
steps.body: Bands may play hymns or special music in the ceremony and festive music at the reception. Ask what each part costs and how long they play.

steps.title: Tornaboda
steps.body: This is a smaller party for close family and friends after the main reception. Decide the guest list and who pays before you send invitations.

name: Indian (Hindu)
blurb: Indian weddings vary a lot by region, religion and family. Many Hindu weddings have several events over a few days, like mehndi, sangeet and the ceremony. Pick only the events your families really hold.

lines.note: ThePricer quotes bridal packages around $350 to $800 at some US providers, and event artists at about $85 to $175 an hour. Ask how many guests get henna.

The four-pillared canopy for the ceremony, with the sacred fire and the priest. ThePricer quotes one decor company at $3,999 and up for a basic mandap with ten centerpieces, and $5,500 and up for a custom one. That is one company, not an average.
The pandit leads the ceremony at the sacred fire. No price found. Ask for the fee and what the ceremony needs.

lines.item: Baraat (groom's procession): dhol player, horse or car
lines.note: The groom's procession to the venue, often with a dhol drummer and family dancing. Some families use a white horse. ThePricer gives no price for it.
Both families gather for performances and dancing. In Punjabi families it is often the biggest event of the week. In some South Indian weddings it is folded into smaller gatherings.
A turmeric paste is applied to the bride and groom, usually at family homes. A private haldi often needs no printed invitation.

lines.item: Food for the extra events (mehndi, sangeet, haldi)
lines.note: Each event adds its own meal. ThePricer's example plan uses $25 a guest for mehndi snacks and $75 to $80 for sangeet. Those are example numbers, not averages.
A sacred necklace is tied around the bride's neck, and sindoor is applied in her hair parting.

lines.item: Extra photo and video for the other events
lines.note: ThePricer lists one photo company at $3,500 for one event and $10,500 for photo and video over several days. That is one company. Ask each photographer to price every event.

milestones.title: Decide which events your families want
milestones.short: There is no single Indian wedding. Pick yours.

steps.title: Customs vary
steps.body: They change by region, religion and language. One guide says South Indian weddings are often shorter, about 2 to 3 days.

steps.title: List the events
steps.body: Common ones are mehndi, haldi, sangeet, baraat, the ceremony and the reception. Ask both families which ones they expect.

steps.title: Count the cost of each
steps.body: Each event adds food, a place and music. Add only the events you will really hold, so the budget stays honest.

milestones.title: Book the pandit and plan the mandap
milestones.short: The ceremony needs a priest, a mandap and a sacred fire.

steps.title: Ask your family for a priest
steps.body: Ask which priest they use. In some South Indian weddings the family priest works out a lucky time for the mangalsutra tying.

steps.title: Ask what the ceremony needs
steps.body: A mandap, a sacred fire and a priest are the core pieces. Ask your venue if a fire is allowed where you plan to hold it.

steps.title: Get the mandap quote in writing
steps.body: Include setup, florals and takedown in the price.

milestones.title: Book the mehndi artist and the dhol player
milestones.short: Two small bookings that fill up around wedding season.

steps.title: Mehndi artist
steps.body: Ask how many guests will get henna and for how long. Event artists are often priced by the hour.

steps.title: Dhol player for the baraat
steps.body: Ask your venue if a procession and drums are allowed outside. Then ask the dhol player what is included.

name: Christian (Protestant)
blurb: Church weddings vary a lot by church. Some only marry members, some charge for the building and the pastor, and many ask for a few counseling sessions first. Ask your church for its wedding guide.

lines.note: Northcross church asks $300, paid at the first meeting, covering the ceremony, rehearsal and counseling. Church by the Park lists $200 for members and $400 for non-members. Two churches, not a survey.
Church by the Park charges members nothing and non-members $400 for the rehearsal and ceremony, plus a $100 damage deposit. Northcross mentions no building fee. Ask your church.
Church by the Park lists $150 for members and $250 for non-members. One church, so ask yours.
Church by the Park lists $100 for members and $150 for non-members for the church, and $75 to $175 more for the hall. One church, so ask yours.

Many churches ask for it. Church by the Park requires at least three sessions. Northcross asks members to take a premarital course and says its Prepare/Enrich tool has an added cost it does not state.

lines.item: Church hall and kitchen for a small reception
lines.note: Church by the Park lists a donation for members and $200 for non-members for the hall and kitchen. If the church has a hall, this can be your venue.

milestones.title: Meet your pastor and ask about the church's rules
milestones.short: The church sets the date, the fees and the steps.

steps.title: Call early
steps.body: Northcross asks for at least six months between first contact and the wedding, and says the pastor you want may be full. Start as early as you can.

steps.title: Ask these questions
steps.body: Do you have to be a member? What are the pastor, building and music fees? Is there a damage deposit? When is each payment due?

steps.title: Check the legal part
steps.body: Texas law lets a licensed or ordained Christian minister or priest perform the ceremony. Ask your pastor to confirm they qualify.

milestones.title: Book your premarital counseling
milestones.short: Many churches want this done before the ceremony is planned.

steps.title: Ask how many sessions
steps.body: One church requires at least three. Another says the number depends on your background and readiness.

steps.title: Fill out the questionnaire early
steps.body: Northcross asks you to complete a pre-marriage questionnaire.

steps.title: Plan the ceremony after
steps.body: Northcross says to plan the ceremony only after counseling is done.

name: Catholic
blurb: A Catholic wedding starts with your parish. The priest or deacon walks you through the steps, and they can differ from parish to parish.

lines.note: A communication tool reviewed with your priest, deacon or a facilitator. The diocese charges a $35 processing fee. Other dioceses may use a different tool.

lines.item: Engaged Encounter retreat or sponsor couple sessions
lines.note: The El Paso diocese asks you to complete one or the other before it issues the marriage license voucher. No price on its pages. Ask the Marriage and Family Life Office.
The El Paso diocese page links NFP classes but gives no details or price. Ask your parish if it is required.
No fee schedule on the diocese pages. One guide says the priest explains church and music fees. Ask early so it is not a surprise.
Music at a Catholic wedding must be sacred, so secular love songs do not fit. The parish music director can help you pick pieces. Ask what the parish charges.
Catholic partners need a recent copy with the church seal from the church where they were baptized. A photocopy will not work. Ask that church what it charges.

milestones.title: Meet your priest or deacon
milestones.short: Everything else follows from this first meeting.

steps.title: Start about six months out
steps.body: The Diocese of El Paso says to begin six months before your date. One guide says up to a year ahead. Earlier gives you more date choices.

steps.title: Ask who runs marriage preparation
steps.body: Ask for the marriage preparation coordinator. At the first meeting the parish tells you which steps it needs.

steps.title: Do this before you book the reception
steps.body: One guide says to meet the priest after you get engaged and before you book the reception venue.

milestones.title: Finish marriage preparation
milestones.short: A short interview, an inventory and one program.

steps.title: Premarital interview
steps.body: Your priest or deacon holds a pre-marital inventory interview with you.

steps.title: FOCCUS inventory
steps.body: Each of you takes it online, then you review it with your priest, deacon or facilitator. The diocese charges $35.

steps.title: Engaged Encounter or sponsor couple
steps.body: Pick one. Turn in your completion certificate to the Marriage and Family Life Office.

steps.title: Ask about the license fee waiver
steps.body: The diocese says completing preparation can get you a waiver of the county marriage license fee. Ask how it works.

milestones.title: Collect your Catholic papers
milestones.short: Some records take weeks to arrive.

steps.title: Baptism certificate
steps.body: Ask the church where you were baptized for a new copy with the seal. One guide says it must be issued within six months of the wedding.

steps.title: Other records the parish may ask for
steps.body: One guide lists First Communion and Confirmation records, and a signed statement that you are free to marry. Your parish will tell you what it needs.

name: Jewish
blurb: Jewish weddings vary by community and family. Many include a ketubah, a chuppah, a ring, blessings over wine and breaking a glass. Talk with your rabbi about what fits you.

lines.note: A marriage contract signed before the ceremony by two witnesses. One guide says the cost varies greatly. One officiant's page says other ketubah websites can charge up to $1,000.
The couple stands under it for the ceremony. Ask your officiant or venue if one is included. One officiant's package includes a simple brass canopy with a white tallit cover.
No price found. Texas law lists a Jewish rabbi as someone who can perform the ceremony. Ask about the fee and what it covers.

lines.item: Kiddush cup, wine and the glass you break
lines.note: A cup for the blessing over wine, and a glass for the end of the ceremony. Some officiants provide them. One includes a kiddush cup as a gift and a glass wrapped in a napkin.

milestones.title: Talk with a rabbi or Jewish officiant
milestones.short: Rabbis and communities do things differently, so ask early.

steps.title: Texas allows it
steps.body: Texas law lists a Jewish rabbi among the people who can perform a wedding ceremony.

steps.title: If one of you is not Jewish
steps.body: Rabbis differ on interfaith weddings. Some decline, some co-officiate with clergy from the other faith, and some officiate alone. Ask each one.

steps.title: Ask what is included
steps.body: One officiant's package includes the chuppah, ketubah, kiddush cup and glass. Ask what yours covers.

milestones.title: Plan the ketubah and the chuppah
milestones.short: Pick the text, the witnesses and the canopy.

steps.title: Choose the ketubah
steps.body: Pick the text and design. Ask who will print and frame it before the ceremony.

steps.title: Choose two witnesses
steps.body: One guide says witnesses are not supposed to be blood relatives, so close friends often do it.

steps.title: Sort out the chuppah
steps.body: Ask your officiant or venue if they have one before you buy or rent one.

name: Muslim
blurb: The faith gives the frame and your culture fills it in, so Muslim weddings look different from family to family. The core is the nikah, the mahr and a walima. The nikah and walima can be on the same day or weeks apart.

lines.item: Mahr (the groom's gift, agreed before the nikah)
lines.note: Agreed in advance and written into the marriage contract. It can be money, gold, jewelry or another gift, and it becomes the bride's own. It is described as a gift, not a payment or a dowry, so it is not a wedding cost. One guide says the couple agrees it, another says the families do, so settle it your own way. Size varies by culture and means.

lines.item: Imam or authorized officiant for the nikah
lines.note: The nikah is usually led by an imam, sheikh or authorized officiant. No price found. Ask your imam about any fee or gift.

lines.item: Nikah contract and civil license paperwork
lines.note: The contract is called the Nikah Nama. In the US a nikah alone is not legally binding, so most couples also file a civil marriage license. The El Paso fee is already in your budget.
A recommended act of generosity and often the biggest gathering. Traditionally hosted by the groom's family, though who pays differs.

lines.item: Henna or mehndi night (if your culture has one)
lines.note: A pre-wedding custom in many cultures. Dress, music, food and number of days vary by culture.

milestones.title: Agree on the mahr
milestones.short: Talk about it early and write it down.

steps.title: Talk about it early
steps.body: The mahr is agreed in advance and recorded in the marriage contract.

steps.title: Decide what it will be
steps.body: It can be money, gold, jewelry or another meaningful gift. The size varies widely by culture and means.

steps.title: Keep it separate from the wedding budget
steps.body: It is the bride's own. It is not a payment for the wedding.

milestones.title: Plan the nikah
milestones.short: Who leads it, who witnesses it and the legal license.

steps.title: Choose who leads the nikah
steps.body: Usually an imam, sheikh or authorized officiant. Ask your community who they recommend.

steps.title: Ask about the wali and witnesses
steps.body: Many guides name a wali for the bride and at least two adult Muslim witnesses. Ask your imam what your community expects.

steps.title: Also file the civil license
steps.body: A nikah alone is not legally binding in the US. The El Paso County Clerk's formal license is $81, and you both go in person.

milestones.title: Plan the walima
milestones.short: The feast can be the same day or later.

steps.title: Pick the day
steps.body: The nikah and walima can be on the same day or separated by days or even weeks.

steps.title: Decide who hosts and pays
steps.body: It is traditionally hosted by the groom's family, but families split this in different ways. Talk it through early, and keep it within your means.

steps.title: Book the place and the food
steps.body: Ask each venue and caterer about your menu and any rules before you sign.

name: Japanese
blurb: A Shinto shrine ceremony is formal and can be followed by a reception with family, friends and coworkers. Families do it differently, and some couples wear a white dress and tuxedo at the reception.

lines.item: Shinto shrine donation or ceremony fee
lines.note: One US shrine lists a minimum donation of $1,000, with kimono and travel added when they apply. Each shrine sets its own rules and fees. Ask for the total.
The bride wears a shiromuku, often with a white hood (wataboshi) over a wig. The groom wears a black montsuki, a haori jacket and hakama pants.
Souvenirs for guests, usually sweets and small trinkets that you choose. Skip it if your reception is small.
One US shrine performs the ceremony at your location. It says travel expenses may apply but gives no amount.

milestones.title: Find a shrine or priest and ask about the legal part
milestones.short: A shrine ceremony and a legal marriage are not always the same thing.

steps.title: Find a shrine or a Shinto priest
steps.body: One US shrine comes to your location. It asks for a reservation and an application form, and says kimono is available on request.

steps.title: Ask what is included
steps.body: Fees, kimono and travel can be separate. Ask for one total.

steps.title: Check who can sign your license
steps.body: Texas lists a minister or priest, a rabbi, an authorized officer of a religious organization, or a judge. Ask the shrine if their priest counts. If not, a judge can sign your license.

milestones.title: Plan the kimono and the hikidemono
milestones.short: Two things that need lead time.

steps.title: Kimono
steps.body: Ask the shrine or a rental shop what is available and when you can try it on. Ask about the wig and headpiece the bride wears.

steps.title: Hikidemono
steps.body: Pick small gifts for guests, usually sweets or trinkets. Order enough for everyone who comes.

name: Chinese
blurb: Chinese weddings vary by region and family. Many couples keep the tea ceremony, red envelopes, a banquet and the double happiness symbol, and shorten or skip the rest.

lines.item: Tea ceremony set (cups, tray and tea)
lines.note: The couple kneels and serves tea to parents and elders, who offer blessings and usually red envelopes or jewelry. Serving order varies by family.

lines.item: Door games: red envelopes and small prizes
lines.note: The groom does challenges to get to the bride. One guide lists envelopes of $288 to $688 for the lead bridesmaid, $88 to $188 for each bridesmaid, and 4 to 8 small group envelopes of $8.80, $18.80 or $28.80. Many Chinese-American families keep it to 20 to 30 minutes.

lines.item: Red qipao (cheongsam) or qun kwa for the bride
lines.note: The bridal qipao is almost always red. Qun kwa is a two-piece red and gold jacket and skirt, the formal choice for Cantonese families from Guangdong and Hong Kong.

The groom's family presents gifts such as tea, lotus seeds, longan, red dates, gold jewelry and cash in red envelopes. The bride's family returns part. Widely done, especially in Cantonese communities.
A professional lion dance is an optional extra. Skip it if it does not matter to your families.

lines.item: Double happiness signs and red decor
lines.note: The double happiness character (囍) appears on nearly every part of a traditional ceremony.

milestones.title: Ask your parents what to keep and pick the date
milestones.short: Do this before you book a venue.

steps.title: Ask which customs matter
steps.body: Han, Cantonese and Northern Chinese customs differ in clothes, food and games. Ask both families which parts they want.

steps.title: Pick a date
steps.body: Many families check the Chinese almanac, sometimes with a fortune teller or an elder. One guide says 8/8 is a popular date.

steps.title: Write down what you keep
steps.body: Tea ceremony, door games, banquet. Decide now and the rest of the plan gets simpler.

milestones.title: Plan the banquet menu with your caterer
milestones.short: Banquets have their own customs.

steps.title: Courses
steps.body: A traditional banquet has 8 to 9 auspicious courses served family style. One guide says Cantonese banquets sometimes run to 10, and Northern ones may reach 12.

steps.title: Avoid the number 4
steps.body: The same guide says the number 4 is avoided. Ask the caterer to count courses that way.

steps.title: Ask about fish and symbolic dishes
steps.body: Ask your caterer which dishes are lucky for your family and what they cost per guest.

milestones.title: Get ready for the tea ceremony and door games
milestones.short: Small things that are easy to forget on the morning.

steps.title: Tea ceremony
steps.body: Make a list of elders in the order they will be served. Serving order and whether families are served together vary by family. Ask your parents.

steps.title: Door games
steps.body: Many Chinese-American families keep them to 20 to 30 minutes. Pick the challenges and fill the red envelopes ahead of time.

steps.title: Red envelopes
steps.body: Count how many you need: one for the lead bridesmaid, one per bridesmaid, and a few small ones for the group.

name: Nigerian
blurb: Nigeria has more than 250 ethnic groups, and Yoruba, Igbo and Hausa-Fulani weddings are quite different. Guides describe a traditional wedding and a church or civil wedding as two separate events. Ask both families which customs to follow.

lines.item: Traditional engagement items (the list from the bride's family)
lines.note: One Yoruba guide lists food such as yams, palm wine, fruit, salt and candy, and goods such as luggage and cookware. Another source says palm wine and kola nuts are common symbolic gifts. The list and who pays differ by group and family, so ask the bride's family.

A gift of gratitude and a promise of support. Its type and value depend on the tradition, and the groom's family usually presents it before the wedding. This is not a vendor cost. Settle it with both families.

lines.item: Aso ebi fabric (matching outfits for family and friends)
lines.note: Families wear matching fabric. The couple's families choose it and each person has it sewn by a tailor they pick. Some couples add an aso ebi card to the invitation.

lines.item: Alaga (two MCs for a Yoruba engagement)
lines.note: Two women MCs, one for each family. For a wedding where only one of you is Nigerian, one Alaga for both families is normally fine.
Yoruba brides and grooms wear items like agbada and gele. Igbo brides wear beaded attire and Igbo grooms a red cap and isiagu fabric. The bride often has a second outfit change.

lines.item: Igbo wine carrying: palm wine and cup
lines.note: In the Igbo ceremony the bride carries a cup of palm wine to her groom among the guests. Skip this if it is not your family's custom.

milestones.title: Decide which customs to follow with both families
milestones.short: Yoruba and Igbo customs differ, so talk first.

steps.title: Know the groups
steps.body: Yoruba, Igbo and Hausa-Fulani are the largest groups in the diaspora. Each has its own ceremony names and customs.

steps.title: If you come from different groups
steps.body: One guide says the bride's culture governs, or the father's if the bride is of mixed heritage. Ask your families before you decide.

steps.title: Choose your events
steps.body: Guides describe a traditional wedding and a church or civil wedding as two separate events. Decide which ones you will hold.

milestones.title: Plan the traditional engagement
milestones.short: The list, the gifts and the people who lead it.

steps.title: Get the list
steps.body: Ask the bride's family what they expect the groom's family to bring.

steps.title: Plan the MCs
steps.body: For a Yoruba engagement, plan two Alaga, one for each family.

steps.title: Plan outfits
steps.body: Traditional dress varies by group. The bride often has a second outfit change.

milestones.title: Choose the aso ebi fabric and add the card
milestones.short: Give guests time to get their outfits sewn.

steps.title: Pick the fabric
steps.body: The couple chooses the colors. Paperlust says there is no single traditional color.

steps.title: Add an insert to the invitation
steps.body: A card can list the fabric colors, vendor contacts and what guests without fabric should wear.

steps.title: Send the fabric early
steps.body: Guests need time to get it sewn by a tailor.

name: Courthouse or civil
blurb: A short ceremony with a judge or officiant, with your license from the El Paso County Clerk. You can still have a party after.

lines.note: Texas lets a current, former or retired federal or state judge perform a ceremony. The El Paso County Clerk's license page lists no ceremony fee. Ask the judge's court what, if anything, they charge.

lines.item: Marriage license if you do not live in Texas
lines.note: The El Paso County Clerk lists $181 for non-Texas residents, next to the $81 formal fee. Ask the Clerk how it applies if only one of you lives outside Texas, and whether it replaces the $81.

milestones.title: Ask a judge's court about a ceremony
milestones.short: Find out who can marry you and when.

steps.title: Know who can marry you
steps.body: Texas law lists a judge, a licensed or ordained Christian minister or priest, a rabbi, or an authorized officer of a religious organization.

steps.title: Call the court
steps.body: The El Paso County Clerk's license page does not say how to book a judge or what it costs. Call the court you have in mind and ask.

steps.title: Pick a few dates
steps.body: Your license is good for 89 days, so choose a date that fits.

milestones.title: Plan your license and ceremony day
milestones.short: Both of you go in person, and the clock starts when it is issued.

steps.title: Go to the Clerk together
steps.body: You both go in person with a valid government photo ID, and you need to know your Social Security number.

steps.title: The 72-hour wait
steps.body: You cannot marry until 72 hours after the license is issued, unless a waiver applies. Waivers include active-duty military, Defense Department employees or contractors, a Twogether in Texas certificate, or a waiver signed by a judge.

steps.title: Use it within 89 days
steps.body: The marriage must happen within 89 days of the license date, with no exceptions.

name: Mixed or our own
blurb: Blending two traditions, or making up your own? Pick any of the others to borrow what you like, then add your own lines and steps. There are no fixed lines here.
